“We won’t just experience 100 years of progress in the twenty-first century — it will be more like 20,000 years of progress.”
_— Ray Kurzweil _



----------View image: (https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/db1950cc-4573-4f46-b7c7-e2f1df0dafe9/image.jpeg?t=1792186464)
Caption: 

# **Friday charts**

When physicist Suvrat Raju saw the results of a [new study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.16733) he co-authored testing AI’s ability to solve physics problems, he was shocked: “I couldn’t sleep properly for a couple of nights,” he [says](https://x.com/Kaju_Nut/status/2110376532267196754?s=20).

Raju, known for his work on black holes, began by asking fellow physicists to develop unpublished problems from their particular sub-fields of expertise. He wanted to see how good standard LLMs like Claude and ChatGPT would be at solving them.

They were shockingly good.

“The best-performing agent, GPT-6-Astra harnessed in Codex, obtains the final answers with a near-perfect accuracy of 98% at an average cost under USD 3 per problem.”

$3!

That is considerably less than the cost of hiring a human to solve the same problems.​​ The paper estimates it would take a physicist a full day to solve the same problems — and considerably longer if they don’t happen to be an expert in the relevant sub-field.

“Frontier agents can now solve verifiable problems in theoretical physics with great accuracy,” the study concluded. “Not only does their breadth exceed that of any individual, but their calculational abilities now match those of world experts even in specialized domains.”

Even the final grade of 98% understates the AI’s achievement. The remaining 2% came from a trick question, included to see if the machines would bend the rules they were given (they did not).

But that’s not the truly shocking part. 

Raju adds that the AIs initially appeared to have solved only 80% of the problems the physicists had challenged them with. As it turns out, there were problems with the problems:  

As we started to investigate the mistakes that the models might have made, the models, especially Astra, insisted that they were right and that it was the expert-supplied answers that were erroneous. When we went back to the experts it turned out, in multiple instances, that the experts found some subtle errors buried deep inside their calculations. As they revised their answers, Astra's score started to inch up and it finally ended up with 98%.
